physics.name: Semiconductor physics
physics.description: Practice the basics of semiconductor physics — band gap, carriers, donors and acceptors — with multiple-choice questions and explanations.
physics.intro:
The properties of a semiconductor are largely determined by its band gap, the energy difference between the valence band and the conduction band. Silicon's band gap is about 1.12 eV at room temperature: not as large as an insulator's, and not zero like a metal's.
Adding impurities produces n-type semiconductors with many electrons or p-type semiconductors with many holes. The temperature dependence of carrier density, mobility, and the difference between drift and diffusion currents form the foundation for understanding the devices you will study later.

pn-junction.name: PN junctions and diodes
pn-junction.description: Learn about the depletion layer of PN junctions, forward and reverse bias, breakdown and diode applications through multiple-choice questions.
pn-junction.intro:
When p-type and n-type semiconductors are joined, carriers diffuse and recombine near the boundary, forming a depletion layer with almost no carriers. A built-in potential develops across the depletion layer, and this is what allows current to flow in only one direction (rectification).
Under forward bias the barrier is lowered and current flows; under reverse bias the depletion layer widens and almost no current flows. If the reverse voltage is increased further, breakdown occurs, a phenomenon used in voltage-regulator (Zener) diodes.

bjt.name: Bipolar transistors
bjt.description: Check the basics of bipolar transistors — NPN/PNP structure, bias conditions and current gain — with multiple-choice questions.
bjt.intro:
A bipolar transistor has a three-layer structure of emitter, base and collector, and both electrons and holes take part in its operation. The base current controls the collector current, amplifying it.
For amplification (the active region), the base-emitter junction is forward-biased and the base-collector junction is reverse-biased. Understand the current gain hFE, the relationship between base width and recombination, and the meaning of the saturation and cutoff regions.

mosfet.name: MOSFET
mosfet.description: Learn MOSFET structure, threshold voltage, gate capacitance and why CMOS uses little power through multiple-choice questions and explanations.
mosfet.intro:
A MOSFET is a transistor that uses the gate voltage to create an inversion layer (channel) at the semiconductor surface and control the current between source and drain. Because the gate is separated by a thin insulator, almost no steady gate current flows.
Threshold voltage, the linear and saturation regions, short-channel effects, and CMOS circuits that combine nMOS and pMOS are key topics for understanding ICs.

logic.name: Logic circuits
logic.description: Check the basics of logic circuits — logic gates, De Morgan's laws and flip-flops — with multiple-choice questions.
logic.intro:
Digital circuits are built from basic gates such as AND, OR and NOT, and their combinations such as NAND, NOR and XOR. Truth tables, Boolean algebra and De Morgan's laws let you simplify logic expressions and replace gates with others.
Also understand the difference between combinational circuits, whose outputs depend only on their inputs, and sequential circuits, which hold state in elements such as flip-flops.
logic.blurb: Logic gates, De Morgan's laws, flip-flops

circuits.name: Circuit and electromagnetism basics
circuits.description: Learn the electrical fundamentals behind electronics — Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, Thevenin's theorem, AC impedance and resonance, RC and RL transients, and electromagnetic induction — with multiple-choice questions.
circuits.intro:
Circuit analysis rests on Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws. With series and parallel combinations, voltage and current dividers, Thevenin's theorem and superposition, even complex circuits can be reduced to simple equivalents for calculation.
In AC circuits, the reactances of inductors and capacitors change with frequency and create phase differences between voltage and current. Impedance, resonance, power factor, transient time constants and the underlying laws of electric fields, magnetic fields and induction are the foundation of every field that deals with electronic circuits, not just semiconductors.

analog.name: Analog and electronic circuits
analog.description: Learn the basics of analog circuits — op-amp properties, inverting amplifier gain and the cutoff frequency of RC filters — with multiple-choice questions.
analog.intro:
Analog circuits handle voltages and currents that change continuously. The operational amplifier, a typical component, is ideally treated as having infinite input impedance, zero output impedance and infinite gain.
The gain of inverting and non-inverting amplifiers with negative feedback, and the time constant and cutoff frequency of RC circuits, are common subjects for calculation questions.

adc-dac.name: A/D and D/A conversion
adc-dac.description: Learn ADC resolution, the sampling theorem, the differences between flash and successive-approximation types, and quantization error through multiple-choice questions.
adc-dac.intro:
An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) turns analog signals into digital values, and a digital-to-analog converter (DAC) does the reverse. They are used wherever real-world signals meet digital processing, such as sensors, communications and audio.
The basic performance measures are resolution (number of bits) and conversion speed. Understand the sampling theorem, quantization error, and the characteristics of each architecture, such as flash, successive approximation and delta-sigma.

dsp.name: Digital Signal Processing Basics
dsp.description: Learn with multiple-choice questions about normalized frequency and the period of discrete-time sinusoids, the unit impulse and unit step, energy and power, linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability, impulse response and convolution, difference equations, DFT frequency resolution and bins, FFT workload, zero padding, spectral leakage and window functions, Parseval's theorem, the z-transform with poles and zeros, FIR and IIR filters, linear phase and group delay, moving averages, the bilinear transform, coefficient quantization, decimation and interpolation, and multiply-accumulate counts and real-time processing.
dsp.intro:
Once an AD converter has turned a signal into a sequence of numbers, processors and FPGAs filter it, analyze its frequency content and change its sampling rate. Digital signal processing runs inside almost every electronic product, from audio and communications to sensors, motor control and measuring instruments.
This topic starts with the normalized frequency and period of discrete-time signals, the unit impulse and step, and energy and power, and then deals with the properties of linear time-invariant systems (linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability), impulse response and convolution, and computing with difference equations. It goes on to check DFT bin spacing and bin indices, the symmetry of the spectra of real signals, FFT workload, zero padding, spectral leakage and window functions, Parseval's theorem, transfer functions with poles and zeros via the z-transform, FIR and IIR filters, linear phase and group delay, moving averages and exponential smoothing, the bilinear transform, coefficient quantization, decimation and interpolation, and estimating multiply-accumulate counts and real-time processing budgets. The values in the calculation questions, including those of the wrong choices, have been checked by computing them in Python (NumPy). The sampling theorem, aliasing, quantization noise, oversampling and delta-sigma ADCs are covered in "A/D and D/A conversion", analog filters and op-amps in "Analog and electronic circuits", OFDM in "Wireless Communication Basics", convolution in CNNs in "Machine Learning Basics", and fixed-point representation in "Computer Arithmetic".

dram.name: DRAM
dram.description: Learn about the DRAM 1T1C cell, why refresh is needed and how reading works through multiple-choice questions.
dram.intro:
DRAM stores one bit with one transistor and one capacitor. Its simple cell structure makes high density easy, so it is widely used as computer main memory.
The charge in the capacitor is gradually lost through leakage current, so the data must be rewritten periodically (refresh). Reading also disturbs the cell's charge, so the data is amplified by a sense amplifier and then written back.

sram-flash.name: SRAM and flash memory
sram-flash.description: Check the 6-transistor SRAM cell, the differences between NAND and NOR flash, and SLC/MLC/TLC with multiple-choice questions.
sram-flash.intro:
SRAM holds data in a latch made of two cross-coupled inverters. It needs no refresh and is fast, so it is used for CPU caches, but each bit takes up more area.
Flash memory is non-volatile: data remains even when the power is off. There is NAND flash, suited to high-capacity storage, and NOR flash, which offers fast random reads. Storing multiple bits per cell (multi-level cells) is also advancing.

emerging-memory.name: Emerging memories
emerging-memory.description: Learn how emerging memories such as MRAM, PCM (phase-change memory), ReRAM and FeRAM store data through multiple-choice questions.
emerging-memory.intro:
To overcome the limits of DRAM and flash memory, memories based on many new principles are being developed. Most are non-volatile and store information not as charge but as differences in resistance or polarization direction.
MRAM uses the magnetization direction of a magnetic tunnel junction, PCM the resistance difference between crystalline and amorphous phases, ReRAM conductive paths in an oxide, and FeRAM the polarization of a ferroelectric. Learn to tell these principles and features apart.

cpu.name: CPUs and architecture
cpu.description: Check CPU basics such as pipelining, cache memory and the von Neumann architecture with multiple-choice questions.
cpu.intro:
A CPU processes a program by repeatedly fetching, decoding and executing instructions. Most computers use the von Neumann architecture, in which programs and data are stored in the same main memory.
Performance-enhancing techniques include pipelining, which overlaps stages of instruction processing; caches, which bridge the speed gap with main memory; and parallel processing with multiple cores. Semiconductor scaling has supported all of these advances.

power.name: Power semiconductors
power.description: Learn the basics of power semiconductors — the strengths of SiC and GaN, IGBT operation and the two-dimensional electron gas in GaN HEMTs — through multiple-choice questions.
power.intro:
Power semiconductors convert and control electric power and are used in inverters, power supplies, electric vehicles and more. They need high breakdown voltage, low on-resistance and fast switching.
In addition to silicon MOSFETs and IGBTs, devices made from SiC and GaN, which have large band gaps and high breakdown fields, are becoming widespread. It is important to understand how material properties relate to device structure.

image-sensor.name: Image sensors and optical devices
image-sensor.description: Check the basics of optical devices — CMOS image sensors, backside illumination (BSI) and what determines LED color — with multiple-choice questions.
image-sensor.intro:
An image sensor converts light into charge with a photodiode in each pixel and reads it out as an electrical signal. CMOS image sensors are now mainstream and widely used in smartphones and automotive cameras.
Backside illumination, which lets light enter from the side opposite the wiring layers, and stacked sensors, which put pixels and circuits on separate chips, have improved performance. Optical devices that convert electricity into light, such as LEDs and lasers, are also part of this topic.
image-sensor.blurb: CMOS image sensors, backside illumination, LEDs

compound.name: Compound semiconductors
compound.description: Learn the features of compound semiconductors such as GaAs, GaN and InP, and the difference between direct and indirect band gaps, through multiple-choice questions.
compound.intro:
Compound semiconductors are made of more than one element, such as GaAs (gallium arsenide) and GaN (gallium nitride). Combinations of group III and group V elements (III-V) are typical.
Some have higher electron mobility than silicon, some have direct band gaps that emit light efficiently, and some have large band gaps. They are used in high-frequency devices, LEDs and lasers, and power devices.
compound.blurb: GaAs, GaN, InP, direct vs indirect gap

finfet.name: Advanced transistors (FinFET and GAA)
finfet.description: Check the key points of advanced transistors — FinFET and GAA structures, short-channel effects, high-k/metal gates and strain engineering — with multiple-choice questions.
finfet.intro:
As transistors shrink, short-channel effects make it harder for the gate to control the channel. FinFETs, whose fin-shaped channel is surrounded by the gate on three sides, solved this, and the design has evolved further into gate-all-around (GAA) transistors that surround the channel completely.
High-k/metal gates, which suppress gate leakage, and strain techniques, which raise mobility, are also important technologies behind advanced transistors.

mems-sensor.name: MEMS and sensors
mems-sensor.description: Learn about MEMS features, capacitive accelerometers, sacrificial-layer etching, the piezoresistive effect and Hall sensors through multiple-choice questions.
mems-sensor.intro:
MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) are devices that use semiconductor microfabrication to build tiny mechanical structures together with electronic circuits. They are widely used as accelerometers, gyroscopes, microphones and pressure sensors in smartphones.
Understand sacrificial-layer etching, which frees movable structures, and the principles that turn displacement, stress or magnetic fields into electrical signals (capacitance, the piezoresistive effect and the Hall effect).

automotive.name: Automotive Semiconductors and Functional Safety
automotive.description: Learn the basics of automotive semiconductors — AEC-Q100 temperature grades, ISO 26262 ASILs with SPFM, LFM and PMHF, safety mechanisms such as lockstep, CAN and automotive Ethernet, load dump and SOTIF — through multiple-choice questions.
automotive.intro:
Automotive semiconductors are used for around 15 years at temperatures ranging from −40 °C to as high as 150 °C, and because their failures can endanger lives, they must meet stricter quality and reliability requirements than consumer parts. The foundation is qualification testing such as AEC-Q100, quality control aiming for zero defects, change notification and traceability.
Beyond that, ISO 26262 functional safety determines an ASIL from the magnitude of the hazard and uses safety mechanisms such as lockstep CPUs, ECC, and voltage and clock monitoring to detect faults and move to a safe state. You will learn the basics of automotive electronic design, from CAN and automotive Ethernet networks and 48 V and 800 V power systems to ADAS sensors and SOTIF.

photonics.name: Silicon photonics
photonics.description: Learn optical components such as silicon waveguides, optical modulators, ring resonators and Ge photodetectors, the basics of telecom wavelength bands, optical interconnects for data centers using WDM and CPO, and key points of fabrication and testing through multiple-choice questions.
photonics.intro:
Silicon photonics integrates waveguides that guide light, modulators, photodetectors and other components on a single chip using the same silicon fabrication technology as CMOS. Silicon barely absorbs light in the 1.31–1.55 µm bands used for communications, and its large refractive index contrast with the surrounding oxide confines light tightly in small circuits.
Data center traffic is surging with AI training and other workloads, and electrical wiring keeps incurring more loss and consuming more power as speeds rise. Optical interconnects such as optical transceivers and CPO, which mounts optical components right next to the switch IC, are drawing attention as the key technology for solving these problems.

quantum.name: Quantum Computing Hardware
quantum.description: Learn quantum computing hardware with multiple-choice questions: qubit superposition and measurement, entanglement, calculations with quantum gates such as X, H, Z and CNOT, T1, T2 and gate fidelity, quantum error correction and the surface code, the superconducting (transmon), trapped-ion, neutral-atom, silicon spin and photonic platforms, and dilution refrigerators and control and readout electronics. Shor's algorithm and post-quantum cryptography are also covered.
quantum.intro:
A quantum computer computes using superpositions of 0 and 1 and quantum entanglement. Its performance is not set by the number of qubits alone, but by gate error rates, how long quantum states can be kept (the coherence time), how the qubits are connected, and how many qubits can be devoted to quantum error correction.
After checking qubit states, measurement probabilities and the effect of quantum gates with small calculations, this topic covers T1, T2 and fidelity and the ideas of the surface code and its threshold. It then turns to the hardware challenges of scaling up: the strengths and weaknesses of superconducting qubits based on Josephson junctions, trapped ions, neutral atoms, silicon spin qubits that can draw on CMOS fabrication, and photonic qubits; dilution refrigerators that cool to about 10 mK; microwave control and dispersive readout; and cryo-CMOS and the heat load of wiring. Why Shor's algorithm threatens public-key cryptography, and post-quantum cryptography as the response, are also covered in relation to the scale of hardware they require.

wafer.name: Silicon wafers
wafer.description: Check the basics of silicon wafers — making single crystals by the CZ and FZ methods, and wafer diameters — with multiple-choice questions.
wafer.intro:
Most semiconductor devices are made on wafers sliced from high-purity single-crystal silicon. Single crystals are grown either by the CZ method, which pulls a crystal from silicon melted in a crucible, or by the FZ method, which uses no crucible.
The grown crystal becomes wafers through slicing, polishing and cleaning. Wafer diameters have kept increasing, and 300 mm wafers are now standard in leading-edge production lines.
wafer.blurb: Single crystals, CZ & FZ methods, diameters

epitaxy.name: Epitaxial growth
epitaxy.description: Check the definition of epitaxial growth, homoepitaxy and heteroepitaxy, lattice mismatch, and MOCVD and MBE with multiple-choice questions.
epitaxy.intro:
Epitaxial growth is a technique for growing a single-crystal thin film on a single-crystal substrate with the same crystal orientation as the substrate. Because it can create layers with precisely controlled impurity concentrations, it is used for power devices, bipolar devices and compound semiconductor devices.
Growing the same material as the substrate is homoepitaxy, and growing a different material is heteroepitaxy. In heteroepitaxy, defects caused by differences in lattice constant (lattice mismatch) must be considered.

oxidation.name: Oxidation and diffusion
oxidation.description: Learn the difference between dry and wet oxidation, how much silicon thermal oxidation consumes, and how diffusion coefficients depend on temperature through multiple-choice questions.
oxidation.intro:
Heating silicon in oxygen or water vapor forms a high-quality SiO2 film on its surface. This is called thermal oxidation, and it has been used for gate insulators, device isolation, masks and more.
Thermal diffusion introduces impurities into silicon at high temperature by atomic diffusion. Because diffusion depends strongly on temperature, careful control of temperature and time is important.
oxidation.blurb: Dry vs wet, thermal oxide, diffusion coefficient

ion-implant.name: Ion implantation
ion-implant.description: Check ion implantation energy and dose, post-implant annealing and how to prevent channeling with multiple-choice questions.
ion-implant.intro:
Ion implantation ionizes impurities, accelerates them with an electric field and drives them into the wafer. Because the dose and depth can be controlled precisely, it is now the main method for introducing dopants.
The implanted ions damage the crystal, so after implantation the wafer is annealed to restore the crystal and electrically activate the dopants. Also understand what determines implant depth and how channeling is prevented.

deposition.name: Deposition (CVD and PVD)
deposition.description: Learn the differences between CVD, PVD and ALD, sputtering and the advantages of plasma CVD through multiple-choice questions.
deposition.intro:
Deposition creates thin films such as insulators, semiconductors and metals on the wafer. It is broadly divided into CVD, which deposits films through chemical reactions of gases, and PVD, which deposits them physically, as in sputtering and evaporation.
As devices shrink and become three-dimensional, ALD, which controls film thickness one atomic layer at a time and coats deep trenches uniformly, is becoming more important.

lithography.name: Lithography
lithography.description: Check the basics of lithography — the resolution formula (k1·λ/NA), the EUV wavelength and positive resist — with multiple-choice questions.
lithography.intro:
Lithography transfers the circuit pattern on a mask (reticle) onto photoresist on the wafer using light. It is the key step that sets the limit of scaling, and exposure tools are among the most advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
Resolution improves with a shorter wavelength λ and a larger numerical aperture NA. ArF excimer laser (193 nm) immersion lithography and EUV lithography with a 13.5 nm wavelength are used for leading-edge products.

etching.name: Etching
etching.description: Learn the basics of etching — anisotropic etching, selectivity and the differences between wet and dry etching — through multiple-choice questions.
etching.intro:
Etching removes the parts of a film not covered by a mask such as resist to form patterns. There is wet etching, which uses chemical solutions, and dry etching, which uses plasma and similar means.
To process fine patterns accurately, anisotropy (etching only vertically) and selectivity (etching only the target film) are important. Reactive ion etching (RIE) is a representative technique.

cmp-cleaning.name: CMP and cleaning
cmp-cleaning.description: Check planarization by CMP, dishing, and the purposes of RCA cleaning (SC-1 and SC-2) with multiple-choice questions.
cmp-cleaning.intro:
CMP (chemical mechanical polishing) planarizes the wafer surface by combining the chemical action of a slurry with mechanical polishing by a pad. It is essential for multilevel interconnects and for forming copper wiring by the damascene process.
Cleaning removes particles, organics, metal contamination and native oxide, and is repeated many times during manufacturing. Learn how the chemicals derived from RCA cleaning are used for different purposes.

interconnect.name: Interconnect processes
interconnect.description: Learn the basics of interconnect processes — copper wiring and the damascene process, low-k materials and RC delay — through multiple-choice questions.
interconnect.intro:
In an IC, transistors are connected by many layers of metal wiring. As scaling progressed, delay caused by wire resistance and capacitance (RC delay) came to limit performance, and wiring materials have been improved accordingly.
Copper wiring, which has lower resistance than aluminum, is hard to dry-etch, so it is made by the damascene process: filling trenches and removing the excess by CMP. Low-k materials with low dielectric constants are used for the interlayer insulators.
interconnect.blurb: Cu wiring, damascene, low-k, RC delay

process-materials.name: Process materials (gases and chemicals)
process-materials.description: Learn the basics of process materials — specialty gases, ultrapure water, etching gases, sputtering targets and high-purity silicon — through multiple-choice questions.
process-materials.intro:
Semiconductor manufacturing uses many materials: high-purity silicon, specialty gases for deposition and etching, chemicals and ultrapure water for cleaning, sputtering targets, photoresists, CMP slurries and more.
Even tiny amounts of impurities can cause defects, so these materials must be extremely pure. Many of the gases are also pyrophoric or toxic, so safe handling is essential.
process-materials.blurb: Special gases, ultrapure water, sputter targets

package.name: Packaging and assembly
package.description: Check the basics of semiconductor packages and assembly — wire bonding, flip chip and BGA — with multiple-choice questions.
package.intro:
A package protects the chip from its environment, connects it electrically to the board and carries away heat. Chips cut from the wafer become products through die bonding, interconnection, encapsulation and other steps.
Chip-to-package connections include wire bonding and flip chip, and package shapes have evolved from types with leads to types like BGA with solder balls on the underside to support higher pin counts.

test.name: Testing and inspection
test.description: Learn the basics of semiconductor testing — wafer test, burn-in and scan test (DFT) — through multiple-choice questions.
test.intro:
Semiconductor products go through several stages of testing during and after manufacturing. Wafer testing before dicing finds defective chips, and final testing after packaging guarantees the characteristics of shipped products.
Burn-in, which removes early failures, and design for testability (DFT), which builds test features into circuits, keep quality high while holding down test costs.

metrology.name: Metrology and analysis
metrology.description: Check the basics of semiconductor metrology and analysis — SEM and TEM, ellipsometry, SIMS and four-point probe — with multiple-choice questions.
metrology.intro:
In semiconductor manufacturing, line widths, film thicknesses, impurity concentrations and defects are measured along the way to confirm that each process is working correctly. The finer the features, the more accurate nanometer-scale measurement must be.
Different methods are used for different purposes: electron microscopes (SEM and TEM) for shape, ellipsometry for film thickness, secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) for impurity profiles, and the four-point probe for sheet resistance.

yield.name: Yield and quality control
yield.description: Check the basics of quality control — yield calculations, the relationship between defect density and chip area, and control charts — with multiple-choice questions.
yield.intro:
Yield is the proportion of good products among those started, and it greatly affects a fab's profitability. With the same defect density, larger chips are more likely to contain a defect, so their yield is lower.
To keep processes stable, data is monitored with statistical methods such as control charts (SPC), so that abnormalities are found and fixed quickly.
yield.blurb: Defect density, chip area, control charts

reliability.name: Reliability
reliability.description: Learn the basics of semiconductor reliability — the bathtub curve, electromigration and MTBF — through multiple-choice questions.
reliability.intro:
Reliability is the ability of a product to keep functioning under specified conditions for a specified time. How the failure rate changes over time is described by the bathtub curve, made up of early-failure, random-failure and wear-out periods.
Failure mechanisms specific to semiconductors include electromigration in interconnects, time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) of gate insulators, and degradation of transistor characteristics. Accelerated tests estimate lifetimes in a short time.

eda.name: IC design flow and EDA
eda.description: Check the IC design flow from specification through RTL design, logic synthesis, place and route, and static timing analysis with multiple-choice questions.
eda.intro:
IC design proceeds by deciding the specification, describing the circuit at register-transfer level (RTL) in a hardware description language, converting it into a netlist of gates by logic synthesis, and creating the layout by place and route.
Each stage requires simulation with EDA tools, static timing analysis (STA) and verification. The larger the design, the greater the verification effort.
eda.blurb: RTL, logic synthesis, place & route, STA

sta-cdc.name: Timing analysis and CDC
sta-cdc.description: Check static timing analysis — setup/hold slack calculation, OCV and multicycle paths — and the design of clock domain crossings using synchronizers and asynchronous FIFOs, with multiple-choice questions.
sta-cdc.intro:
For a synchronous circuit to work correctly, data must arrive on every path between flip-flops in time to meet setup and hold times. Static timing analysis (STA) computes the slack of each path from the clock and input/output delay constraints given in SDC, accounting for skew, jitter and manufacturing variation, and finds violations.
Between asynchronous clocks, on the other hand, timing cannot be guaranteed and metastability is unavoidable. Designing and verifying clock domain crossings (CDC) that pass signals safely — with two-flip-flop synchronizers, handshakes and asynchronous FIFOs with Gray code pointers — is also a fundamental part of logic design.

cleanroom.name: Cleanrooms and equipment
cleanroom.description: Learn the basics of fab environments and equipment — cleanroom cleanliness, yellow rooms and FOUPs — through multiple-choice questions.
cleanroom.intro:
In semiconductor manufacturing even tiny particles can cause defects, so work is done in cleanrooms where airborne particles are kept extremely low. Cleanliness is expressed as the number of particles in a given volume of air.
In 300 mm fabs, wafers are carried automatically in sealed containers called FOUPs, and the usual approach is to keep only the inside of equipment at very high cleanliness.

ehs.name: Environment, health and safety
ehs.description: Check the basics of fab environment and safety — the hazards of hydrofluoric acid, SDSs, and PFC gases and global warming — with multiple-choice questions.
ehs.intro:
Semiconductor fabs use many chemicals such as hydrofluoric acid, as well as toxic or flammable specialty gases. Understanding the hazards of chemicals and handling them correctly according to their SDS (safety data sheet) is fundamental.
Exhaust gases are treated by abatement systems before release. Reducing emissions of greenhouse gases such as PFCs, used for etching and chamber cleaning, is also an important issue.

industry.name: Semiconductor industry and market
industry.description: Learn the structure and basic terms of the semiconductor industry — foundry, fabless, IDM and Moore's law — through multiple-choice questions.
industry.intro:
In addition to IDMs, which handle everything from design to manufacturing and sales in-house, the semiconductor industry has seen a growing division of labor between fabless companies, which own no fabs and focus on design, and foundries, which specialize in contract manufacturing.
Moore's law, which says that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles at regular intervals, has long served as a benchmark for the industry's technology development.

advanced-packaging.name: Advanced packaging (3D and chiplets)
advanced-packaging.description: Check 3D integration and advanced packaging technologies such as chiplets, TSVs (through-silicon vias) and HBM with multiple-choice questions.
advanced-packaging.intro:
As scaling alone has become less able to raise performance, technologies that combine several chips in one package are attracting attention. Building systems from small chips divided by function (chiplets) also has advantages in yield and cost.
3D integration, which stacks chips vertically with TSVs, and 2.5D integration, which places a processor and HBM side by side on an interposer, are used in high-performance chips for AI.

datasheet.name: How to read datasheets
datasheet.description: Learn how to read datasheets — absolute maximum ratings versus recommended operating conditions, typ versus min/max values, I/O levels and timing, thermal resistance and junction temperature, and key MOSFET and op-amp parameters — with multiple-choice questions.
datasheet.intro:
The datasheet is the most dependable reference when selecting parts and designing circuits. Its numbers, however, cannot simply be used as written. The basics are to distinguish absolute maximum ratings, the limits for avoiding damage, from recommended operating conditions, within which performance is guaranteed; to distinguish guaranteed min/max values from typ values, which are only a guide; and to read the test conditions, such as temperature and supply voltage, attached to each value.
You will also learn input/output voltage levels and noise margin, timing such as setup and hold, and junction-temperature calculations using thermal resistance, as well as how to read the key parameters of MOSFETs, op-amps, regulators and A/D converters, and assembly-related information such as packages, ESD robustness and moisture sensitivity.

computer-arithmetic.name: Computer Arithmetic
computer-arithmetic.description: Learn computer arithmetic with multiple-choice questions: fixed point, IEEE 754 floating point (normalization, subnormals, rounding, special values), rounding error and cancellation, bfloat16 and INT8, multipliers and carry-lookahead adders.
computer-arithmetic.intro:
Computers represent numbers with a finite number of bits, so both range and precision are limited. Whereas fixed point keeps the binary point in a fixed position, IEEE 754 floating point splits a number into sign, exponent and significand to cover values from tiny to huge. It is important to understand normalization, subnormal numbers, rounding modes and special values such as infinity and NaN.
Floating-point calculations incur rounding error, and subtracting nearly equal numbers causes cancellation, which loses significant digits. AI uses short formats such as bfloat16, FP16, FP8 and INT8. Along with number formats, this topic covers the circuits that implement arithmetic in hardware, such as multipliers, dividers and carry-lookahead adders.

probability-statistics.name: Probability, Statistics and Queueing
probability-statistics.description: Learn probability, statistics and queueing with multiple-choice questions centered on calculations: permutations and combinations, the inclusion-exclusion principle, complementary events and conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, expected value, variance and standard deviation, the binomial, Poisson, uniform, normal and exponential distributions, the median, quartiles and box plots, the correlation coefficient and regression lines, the standard error and confidence intervals, hypothesis testing and p-values, queues (M/M/1) and Little's law, and the probabilities of bit errors and sampling inspection.
probability-statistics.intro:
"What is the probability that it happens at least once?" "What is the probability that a part judged positive is really defective?" "How much longer does the wait get when server utilization rises from 80% to 90%?" Probability and statistics answer questions like these. They are the common tools for handling variation and uncertainty with numbers in many fields of engineering: semiconductor yield and reliability, bit errors in communication, computer performance evaluation, machine learning and more.
This topic covers counting cases with permutations and combinations, the inclusion-exclusion principle, complementary events and independence, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, expected value and its linearity, and variance and standard deviation. It then checks the properties of the binomial, Poisson, uniform, normal (the 68-95-99.7 rule and standardization) and exponential (memorylessness) distributions through calculations. On the statistics side, it deals with the median, quartiles and box plots, the correlation coefficient and the slope of the regression line, the standard error and confidence intervals, and p-values and type I and type II errors in hypothesis testing. The last part calculates utilization, average waiting time and response time with the M/M/1 queueing model, covers Little's law and the effect of how queues are formed, and applies these ideas to the probabilities of bit errors, parity checks and sampling inspection. It helps with the applied mathematics (probability, statistics and queueing) of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations. Control charts and process capability indices are covered in "Yield and quality control", failure rates and the Weibull distribution in "Reliability", confusion matrices and machine learning models in "Machine Learning Basics", and availability calculations in "System Architecture and Reliability".
probability-statistics.blurb: Counting, distributions, estimation and testing, M/M/1

info-theory.name: Information Theory and Coding Basics
info-theory.description: Learn information theory and coding with multiple-choice questions centered on calculations: self-information and entropy, mutual information, redundancy, fixed-length and variable-length codes, prefix codes and the Kraft inequality, the average code length and efficiency of Huffman codes, run-length encoding, the LZ77 method, lossless and lossy compression, parity and vertical and horizontal parity, checksums, CRC calculation, Hamming distance and error detection and correction capability, Hamming codes and SECDED, code rate, interleaving, ARQ and FEC, the capacity of the binary symmetric channel, the channel coding theorem, and Gray code conversion.
info-theory.intro:
"How many bits is this information worth?" "How small can these data be made?" "How can bits corrupted by noise be found and fixed?" Information theory and coding theory, founded by Shannon, answer questions like these. They are at work everywhere in computers and communication: file compression, memory ECC, error correction on communication channels, CRCs in storage devices and more.
This topic checks through calculations the amount of information −log₂ p and entropy, the condition for maximum entropy, conditional entropy and mutual information, redundancy, and the number of bits needed to distinguish items. It goes on to fixed-length and variable-length codes, prefix codes and the Kraft inequality, how to build a Huffman code and its average code length, efficiency compared with the entropy, the effect of coding symbols together, run-length encoding and the LZ77 method, and when to use lossless or lossy compression. The second half deals with parity and vertical and horizontal parity, the weakness of checksums, calculating CRC check bits and detecting burst errors, Hamming distance and the number of bit errors that can be detected and corrected, locating an error with the syndrome of the Hamming (7, 4) code, the number of SECDED check bits, code rate, interleaving, ARQ and FEC, and the capacity of the binary symmetric channel and the channel coding theorem, and it ends with Gray code conversion. It helps with the basic theory (information theory and communication theory) of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations. The values in the calculation questions, including those of the wrong choices and the Huffman trees, have been checked by computing them in Python. Binary numbers and floating point are covered in "Computer Arithmetic"; calculating a parity bit and the properties of Gray code in "Logic circuits"; converting binary to Gray code in "Timing analysis and CDC"; the probability of errors that parity misses in "Probability, Statistics and Queueing"; channel capacity with the Shannon–Hartley theorem in "Wireless Communication Basics"; memory ECC in "DRAM"; 8b/10b encoding and the CRC of PCI Express in "I/O Interfaces & Buses"; Base64 and gzip in "Web Technology Basics"; cross-entropy in "Machine Learning Basics"; and hashes and cryptography in "Information Security Basics".
info-theory.blurb: Entropy, Huffman codes, Hamming codes, CRC

isa-assembly.name: ISA & Assembly
isa-assembly.description: Learn the basics of instruction sets and assembly language with multiple-choice questions: instruction formats, addressing modes, core RISC-V instructions, calling conventions and stack frames.
isa-assembly.intro:
An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the contract between software and hardware. It defines which instructions exist, how they are encoded as bits, and how registers and memory are specified. Any CPU that honors the same ISA can run the same programs, however different its internals.
Assembly language writes machine instructions in human-readable form. Knowing the core RISC-V instructions, register usage, how arguments and return values are passed between functions (the calling convention) and how stack frames are built shows you what compilers generate and how programs actually run on a CPU.

compiler.name: Compilers
compiler.description: Learn how compilers work with multiple-choice questions: lexing and parsing, SSA-form intermediate representations, optimizations such as constant folding and loop unrolling, and register allocation.
compiler.intro:
A compiler translates programs written by people into machine code a CPU can execute. It passes through lexical analysis, which splits source code into tokens; parsing, which builds a tree according to the grammar; and semantic analysis, which checks types and names, before converting the program to an intermediate representation (IR).
On the IR it applies optimizations such as constant folding, common subexpression elimination, inlining, loop unrolling and vectorization, then generates code suited to the CPU through register allocation and instruction scheduling. Understanding these optimizations shows how to write fast code and how to get the most out of the hardware.

linker-loader.name: Linkers, Loaders & Executables
linker-loader.description: Learn about object files and the ELF format, symbol resolution and relocation, static and dynamic linking, and process memory layout with multiple-choice questions.
linker-loader.intro:
What a compiler produces is an object file, which cannot run on its own. A linker gathers object files and libraries, binds names of functions and variables (symbols) to actual addresses (symbol resolution), patches those addresses into instructions (relocation), and produces an executable.
A loader reads the executable into memory, sets up the text, data, BSS, heap and stack regions, and starts the program. Dynamic linking, which binds libraries at run time, and position-independent code (PIC), which runs at any address, help both to save memory and to improve security.

os-hardware.name: OS & Hardware
os-hardware.description: Learn the boundary between operating systems and hardware with multiple-choice questions: interrupts and exceptions, privilege modes and system calls, page tables and page faults, context switches and virtualization.
os-hardware.intro:
An operating system (OS) is software that lets many programs share hardware such as CPUs, memory and I/O devices safely. To support it, CPUs provide privileged modes usable only by the OS, interrupt and exception mechanisms, and hardware that walks page tables for virtual memory.
Applications ask the OS for services through system calls; the OS switches between programs on timer interrupts (context switches) and responds to page faults by bringing the needed pages into memory. From device drivers and memory-mapped I/O to virtualization with hypervisors, this topic covers how hardware and software cooperate.

linux-cli.name: Linux and Command-Line Basics
linux-cli.description: Learn with multiple-choice questions about the Linux directory layout and paths, hard and symbolic links, wildcards, permissions with chmod and umask, sudo and setuid, redirection and pipes, grep and regular expressions, sort, uniq, cut, sed, awk and find, signals and job control, exit status with && and ||, quoting, arguments, conditions and loops in shell scripts, PATH and environment variables, package management, systemd, cron, df and du, SSH public-key authentication, tar, and basic Git operations.
linux-cli.intro:
Most servers and clouds run Linux, and EDA tools for logic synthesis, circuit simulation and the like are also normally used on Linux servers. There, daily work means typing commands into a shell rather than clicking buttons: inspecting files, filtering logs, and leaving long jobs running after disconnecting.
This topic covers the directory layout, absolute and relative paths, hidden files, hard and symbolic links, wildcards, rwx permissions and their octal notation, umask, execute permission on directories, and sudo and setuid. It then deals with redirection and pipes, grep and regular expressions, counting with sort and uniq, tail -f, cut, sed, awk, find, kill and signals, Ctrl+Z with bg and fg, nohup, exit status with && and ||, quoting and variable expansion, script arguments, conditions and loops, and PATH and export, and finally checks package management, systemctl, cron, df and du, SSH keys, tar, and Git add, commit and push with .gitignore. Command behavior follows bash and the GNU commands (coreutils, grep, sed, findutils, tar), and the outputs in the questions have been checked by actually running them on Linux. How processes and virtual memory work is covered in "OS & Hardware", port numbers and DNS in "Computer Networking Basics", access-control principles in "Information Security Basics", and Git merges and development practices in "Software Development and Project Management".

memory-hierarchy.name: Memory Hierarchy
memory-hierarchy.description: Learn about the memory hierarchy and performance with multiple-choice questions: cache organization, tag/set/offset calculations, replacement and write policies, the three types of misses, and average memory access time.
memory-hierarchy.intro:
A CPU operation takes well under a nanosecond, yet reading data from DRAM main memory takes tens to a hundred nanoseconds. To bridge this gap, computers stack a hierarchy from small, fast caches to large, slow main memory and storage, keeping frequently used data in the fast levels.
Caches work because programs exhibit temporal and spatial locality. Understanding direct-mapped and set-associative organizations, splitting addresses into tag, index and offset, the three types of misses and how to compute average memory access time explains why data layout and loop order can change performance several times over.
memory-hierarchy.blurb: Caches, replacement policies, 3 types of misses

multicore-sync.name: Multicore & Synchronization
multicore-sync.description: Learn about the MESI protocol, memory consistency models, atomic instructions such as CAS and LL/SC, locks and memory barriers, false sharing and data races with multiple-choice questions.
multicore-sync.intro:
In a multicore CPU, several cores on one chip share the same memory while each keeps its own caches. Coherence protocols such as MESI manage cache-line states so that no core keeps using stale data after another core writes it.
Beyond that, you need to understand memory consistency models, which define the order in which writes become visible to other cores, atomic instructions that let cores update values safely, and locks and memory barriers. This topic also covers pitfalls such as false sharing and data races, which make programs that look correct run slowly or misbehave.

gpu-programming.name: GPU Programming
gpu-programming.description: Learn the principles of GPU programming with multiple-choice questions: the grid/block/warp hierarchy, shared memory, coalesced memory access, warp divergence and occupancy.
gpu-programming.intro:
A GPU is a processor that excels at running thousands to tens of thousands of threads simultaneously, applying the same operation to large amounts of data. Programs express parallelism in a hierarchy of grids, blocks and threads, and the hardware executes groups of about 32 threads, called warps, in lockstep.
Getting performance requires coalesced memory access, where neighboring threads read neighboring addresses; on-chip shared memory used within a block; avoiding divergence within a warp; and enough occupancy to hide memory latency. This topic focuses on principles that do not depend on product generations.

ai-stack.name: AI Hardware & Software Stack
ai-stack.description: Learn about AI hardware and software with multiple-choice questions: inference versus training, quantization, arithmetic intensity and the roofline model, systolic arrays, operator fusion and tiling.
ai-stack.intro:
Most of the computation in neural networks is large matrix multiply-accumulate. AI hardware therefore lines up many multiply-accumulate units and is designed to reuse data as much as possible to reduce traffic to memory. Training requires far more computation and memory than inference, and also needs higher numerical precision.
Performance is not set by the number of compute units alone. Arithmetic intensity, the amount of computation per byte of data, together with the roofline model, shows whether a workload is limited by compute or by memory bandwidth. This topic also covers how AI compilers and inference runtimes unlock hardware performance through quantization, operator fusion and tiling.

machine-learning.name: Machine Learning Basics
machine-learning.description: Learn machine learning with multiple-choice questions, including calculations: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, classification and regression, k-means and principal component analysis, cross-validation, overfitting and regularization, confusion matrices with precision, recall and F1 score, models such as decision trees, SVMs and naive Bayes, the forward pass and activation functions of neural networks, gradient descent and backpropagation, CNNs, RNNs and the Transformer, transfer learning and generative models.
machine-learning.intro:
Machine learning is the technology of learning rules automatically from data in order to make predictions and classifications. There is supervised learning, which uses correct-answer labels; unsupervised learning, which finds structure in unlabeled data; and reinforcement learning, which learns actions from rewards. Whatever the method, what matters is how accurately the model predicts on data not used for training (generalization performance).
This topic covers, mainly through calculation questions, splitting data into training, validation and test sets and cross-validation, overfitting and the bias–variance trade-off, regularization and dropout, precision, recall and the F1 score computed from a confusion matrix, the ROC curve and the mean squared error. After representative models such as linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, k-nearest neighbors, SVMs and naive Bayes, it goes on to the forward pass of neural networks, activation functions, loss functions, gradient descent and backpropagation, mini-batches and epochs, output sizes in CNNs, RNNs and the Transformer, transfer learning, generative models and the tokens of LLMs. It also helps with the AI sections of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations, and with the JDLA Deep Learning for GENERAL (G-kentei) certificate.
machine-learning.blurb: Learning types, evaluation metrics and neural networks

embedded.name: Embedded Systems & Firmware
embedded.description: Learn the basics of embedded systems and firmware with multiple-choice questions: register access and bit manipulation, GPIO and timers, interrupt-handler pitfalls, UART, SPI and I2C, RTOSes and watchdogs.
embedded.intro:
Inside appliances, cars and industrial equipment, firmware running on microcontrollers controls the device. Firmware reads and writes peripheral registers directly, using bit manipulation to change specific bits, to drive pin I/O (GPIO), timers and communication peripherals.
Embedded code has its own rules, such as keeping interrupt handlers short and declaring shared variables volatile. From UART, SPI and I2C communication and RTOSes that switch tasks by priority to the boot loader that runs first at power-on and the watchdog that recovers from runaway code, this topic covers the software closest to the hardware.

hdl-verification.name: HDL & Verification
hdl-verification.description: Learn Verilog and SystemVerilog basics with multiple-choice questions: synthesizable code, blocking versus nonblocking assignments, unintended latches, state machines, testbenches and assertions.
hdl-verification.intro:
Digital circuits are written in hardware description languages (HDLs) such as Verilog and SystemVerilog. The code looks like a program, but it describes hardware that operates concurrently. HDLs have their own rules: which constructs can be synthesized into circuits, when to use blocking versus nonblocking assignments, and how missing conditions create unintended latches.
Whether a circuit is correct is checked with a testbench that drives inputs. From writing state machines and automatically checking properties with assertions to measuring verification completeness with coverage and generating circuits from C with high-level synthesis, this topic covers the basics of designing and verifying with HDLs.

io-interface.name: I/O Interfaces & Buses
io-interface.description: Learn about I/O interfaces and buses with multiple-choice questions: PCI Express lanes and bandwidth calculations, SerDes serial links, USB, on-chip buses such as AXI, CXL, and bandwidth versus latency.
io-interface.intro:
Inside a computer, components such as the CPU, memory, GPU, storage and network are connected by various interfaces. For high-speed links, serial transmission, which sends very fast signals over a few wires, has replaced parallel buses with many wires, enabled by transceiver circuits called SerDes.
This topic covers calculating bandwidth from PCI Express lane count and per-lane speed, encoding efficiency, USB basics, on-chip buses such as AXI that connect blocks within a chip, and CXL for sharing memory. Understanding that bandwidth and latency are different quantities reveals what actually limits performance.

network.name: Computer Networking Basics
network.description: Learn computer networking with multiple-choice questions: the OSI reference model and TCP/IP, IP addressing and subnet calculations, ARP and routing, TCP and UDP, DNS, DHCP and TLS, transfer-time calculations, wireless LAN, firewalls and VPNs.
network.intro:
Even opening a single web page sets many mechanisms to work in turn: looking up an address from a name, choosing a route, delivering data reliably and protecting it with encryption. Computer networks organize these functions into layers, with each layer taking care of its own role only.
This topic covers the OSI reference model and the TCP/IP layers, MAC addresses and switches, IP addresses and subnet mask calculations, ARP and routing, TCP's three-way handshake, flow control and congestion control, and DNS, DHCP and TLS. It also covers calculating transfer times from bandwidth and latency, and the basics of wireless LAN, firewalls and VPNs, which helps with the network section of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental Information Technology Engineer Examination.

web-tech.name: Web Technology Basics
web-tech.description: Learn how the web works with multiple-choice questions: HTTP requests and responses, methods and status codes, headers and cache control, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, cookies and sessions, JWT, OAuth and OpenID Connect, REST APIs, URLs and JSON, WebSocket and webhooks, the DOM and CSS, the event loop, the same-origin policy and CORS, Service Workers, CDNs and compression, Core Web Vitals, web servers and reverse proxies, and SSR, CSR and SSG.
web-tech.intro:
When you open a URL in a browser, an HTTP request reaches a server, and the browser builds the screen from the HTML, CSS and JavaScript that come back. The web is made of many technologies working together: cookies that keep you logged in, APIs that connect to other services, and caches and CDNs that speed up display.
This topic covers the shape of HTTP requests and responses, the safety and idempotency of methods, status codes, cache control with headers, and the differences between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. It then deals with managing state with cookies, sessions and JWTs, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, REST APIs, the structure of URLs, percent-encoding and JSON, and WebSocket and webhooks. On the browser side, it covers the DOM, the CSS box model and specificity, the processing up to the first display, the JavaScript event loop, the same-origin policy and CORS, Service Workers and responsive design; on the delivery side, browser and CDN caches, compression and transfer-time calculations, Core Web Vitals, image formats, web and application servers, reverse proxies, and SSR, CSR and SSG. It also helps with the network and web-system sections of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations. How TCP/IP, DNS and TLS work is covered in "Computer Networking Basics", attacks and countermeasures such as XSS, CSRF and SQL injection in "Information Security Basics", and the design of load balancing and redundancy in "System Architecture and Reliability".

wireless.name: Wireless Communication Basics
wireless.description: Learn wireless communication with multiple-choice questions: wavelength and frequency, dBm and link budgets, free-space path loss and fading, ASK, PSK and QAM with symbol rates, Shannon's theorem, OFDM and OFDMA, MIMO and beamforming, the hidden node problem in wireless LANs, BLE, LPWA and NFC, LNAs, mixers, PAs and noise figure, and superheterodyne and direct-conversion receivers.
wireless.intro:
Smartphones, wireless LANs and IoT devices put information onto radio waves and pick extremely weak signals out of noise. Their performance is set by the combination of communication schemes such as modulation and multiple access, RF circuits such as amplifiers, mixers and filters, and the semiconductor devices that make them possible.
This topic covers, with calculation questions, radio basics such as frequency and wavelength, link budgets in dB and dBm, free-space path loss, multipath fading and Doppler shift, and goes on to ASK, FSK, PSK and QAM, symbol rate and bit rate, Shannon's theorem, OFDM and the cyclic prefix, CDMA and OFDMA, and MIMO and beamforming. It also covers wireless LAN standards and the hidden node problem, WPA3, BLE, LPWA, NFC and GNSS, the concepts behind 4G LTE and 5G NR, the roles of LNAs, mixers, PAs and duplexers, noise figure and Friis's formula, receiver sensitivity, superheterodyne and direct-conversion receivers, and why compound semiconductors are used for PAs.
wireless.blurb: Modulation, OFDM, MIMO and RF circuits

security.name: Information Security Basics
security.description: Learn information security with multiple-choice questions: the CIA triad and risk, symmetric-key and public-key cryptography, hash functions and digital signatures, authentication and multi-factor authentication, access control, malware and phishing, web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS, and backups and incident response.
security.intro:
Protecting information means keeping it in a state where only authorized people can see it (confidentiality), its contents stay correct (integrity) and it can be used when needed (availability). To achieve this, technologies such as encryption, hash functions and digital signatures are combined with authentication, access control, backups and organizational management.
This topic covers threats, vulnerabilities and risk and how to respond to risk, when to use symmetric-key or public-key cryptography and how to calculate the number of keys, hash functions and password storage, digital signatures and certificates, multi-factor authentication and the error rates of biometrics, and the principle of least privilege. It also explains malware, phishing and web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting in terms of how they work and how to defend against them, which helps with the security section of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations. Hardware-related security is covered in the Hardware Security topic.

cryptography.name: Applied Cryptography
cryptography.description: Learn with multiple-choice questions, including calculations: block and stream ciphers, AES, modes of operation (ECB, CBC, CTR and GCM), initialization vectors and nonces, padding oracle attacks, key length and brute-force effort, SHA-2 and SHA-3, length extension attacks and HMAC, birthday-attack calculations, key derivation functions, RSA and Diffie–Hellman key exchange worked through with small numbers, elliptic-curve key lengths, forward secrecy, certificate authorities and certificate chains, Certificate Transparency, TLS 1.3, 0-RTT and replay, mutual TLS, Grover's algorithm and key length, ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA, hybrid key exchange, HSMs, envelope encryption, key rotation and crypto agility.
cryptography.intro:
A secure algorithm alone does not make cryptography useful. Mistakes in how it is used, such as reusing a nonce, encrypting in ECB mode or failing to check the host name on a certificate, can easily break even strong cryptography. This topic goes one level deeper into how cryptography is combined and used inside real systems and protocols.
It starts with symmetric-key cryptography: block and stream ciphers, the block and key lengths of AES, modes of operation (ECB, CBC, CTR and GCM) and the requirements on initialization vectors and nonces, padding and padding oracle attacks, and authenticated encryption (AEAD), checking by calculation how plaintext leaks when a nonce is reused in CTR mode. It continues with SHA-2 and SHA-3, length extension attacks and HMAC, the limits of 64-bit blocks under the birthday attack, and key derivation functions, then works through RSA and Diffie–Hellman key exchange with small numbers to examine the discrete logarithm problem, man-in-the-middle attacks, guideline key lengths for elliptic-curve cryptography, forward secrecy and the handling of the random number in ECDSA. The second half covers certificate authorities and certificate chains, host name checks, Certificate Transparency, the changes and cipher suites of TLS 1.3, replay with 0-RTT and mutual TLS, and, for post-quantum cryptography, Grover's algorithm and key length, ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA standardized in August 2024, key encapsulation mechanisms, hybrid key exchange and how to think about the timing of migration. It ends with key management: HSMs, envelope encryption, key rotation and crypto agility. It helps with the security sections of IT certification exams such as Japan's Applied Information Technology Engineer Examination and Registered Information Security Specialist Examination. The values in the calculation questions, including those of the wrong choices, have been checked by computing them in Python. The basics of symmetric-key and public-key cryptography, counting keys, the properties of hash functions and password storage, and the difference between digital signatures and MACs are covered in "Information Security Basics"; side-channel attacks and constant-time implementation, AES-NI, TPMs and true random number generators in "Hardware Security"; Shor's algorithm and the scale of quantum computers in "Quantum Computing Hardware"; the number of round trips in TLS and what HTTPS protects in "Computer Networking Basics"; JWT and OAuth in "Web Technology Basics"; and entropy in "Information Theory and Coding Basics".
cryptography.blurb: AES, modes of operation, RSA, TLS 1.3, post-quantum crypto

database.name: Database Basics
database.description: Learn databases with multiple-choice questions: tables and keys in relational databases, SQL searches, aggregation, joins and subqueries, normalization and E-R diagrams, transactions and the ACID properties, concurrency problems and isolation levels, locks and deadlocks, recovery from failures, indexes and NoSQL.
database.intro:
From an online shop's inventory to bank accounts, most information systems entrust their data to a database. A relational database holds data as tables, links tables with primary keys and foreign keys, and retrieves and updates the data it needs with a language called SQL.
This topic covers searching with SQL SELECT statements, aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING, inner and outer joins, and subqueries, counting the results on small example tables. It also covers normalization and E-R diagrams for splitting tables correctly, the ACID properties of transactions, concurrency problems such as lost updates and dirty reads and the isolation levels that prevent them, locks and deadlocks, recovery from failures using logs, how indexes work, and the ideas behind NoSQL, which helps with the database section of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations.

algorithms.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
algorithms.description: Learn data structures and algorithms with multiple-choice questions: time complexity and Big-O notation, arrays and linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, binary search, how sorting algorithms work and their stability, binary search trees and heaps, graph search and shortest paths, and recursion, dynamic programming and greedy algorithms, including how they relate to caches and GPUs.
algorithms.intro:
Programs that solve the same problem can differ in speed by orders of magnitude as the data grows, depending on the data structures and algorithms they use. Estimating how the work grows with time complexity and choosing structures that fit how the data is used are the starting points for fast programs.
This topic covers basic data structures such as arrays and linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, binary search trees and heaps, and graph representations, along with binary search; sorting algorithms such as bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick and heap sort; breadth-first search, depth-first search and Dijkstra's algorithm; and recursion, dynamic programming and greedy algorithms, mainly through calculation questions that trace each step. It also helps with the algorithms section of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations. In addition, it covers the link to hardware performance, such as cache-friendly data layouts and parallel sorting on GPUs.

programming.name: Programming Basics (Pseudocode Tracing)
programming.description: Learn to trace short programs line by line with multiple-choice questions, written in the same pseudo-language as Part B of Japan's Fundamental Information Technology Engineer Examination. Topics include variables and assignment, loops and conditional branching, arrays and strings, integer division and remainders, recursion, bitwise operations, stacks and queues, linked lists, off-by-one errors, short-circuit evaluation, floating-point error, and classes and instances.
programming.intro:
To read a program's behavior accurately, you need to be able to follow by hand (trace) how the values of variables change line by line. Small oversights, such as miscounting a loop by one, losing a value through the order of assignments, or forgetting that integer division discards the fractional part, lead to wrong results and bugs.
This topic centers on questions that ask you to trace short programs and give the result. The programs follow the pseudo-language used in Part B of Japan's Fundamental Information Technology Engineer Examination, with type declarations, assignment with ←, if, while and for, and array indices that start at 1. The wrong choices are values produced by typical mistakes, such as getting the final value of a loop wrong or misreading operator precedence, and the explanations show which mistake each choice comes from.

c-language.name: C Programming Basics
c-language.description: Learn C with multiple-choice questions that trace short code: integer type sizes and fixed-width types, integer promotion and signed/unsigned conversion, operator precedence, bitwise operations, switch statements, pass by value and pointers, static variables, arrays and pointer arithmetic, strings and sizeof, const, function pointers, malloc, free and memory leaks, dangling pointers, buffer overflows, struct padding, unions and endianness, bit-fields, macros and conditional compilation, volatile, and undefined behavior.
c-language.intro:
C is still widely used for software close to the hardware, such as operating systems, device drivers and microcontroller firmware. It lets you handle memory addresses directly and write fast code, but it also has many rules whose mistakes are hard to notice unless you know them: the size of int differs between implementations, types change in the middle of a calculation, and nothing stops a program that writes past the end of an array.
This topic centers on questions that trace the output of short code when it is actually run. It covers integer type sizes and the fixed-width integer types of stdint.h, integer division, integer promotion and signed/unsigned comparison, operator precedence, bitwise operations, short-circuit evaluation, fall-through in switch statements, pass by value and passing pointers, static variables and lifetimes, pointer arithmetic and arrays, the layout of two-dimensional arrays, strings with strlen and sizeof, where to put const, and function pointers. It then deals with malloc and free, memory leaks, dangling pointers, buffer overflows, null pointers, struct padding, unions and endianness, bit-fields, macros and include guards, conditional compilation, volatile in embedded code, and undefined behavior and compiler optimization. The program outputs have been checked by actually compiling the code with gcc on x86-64 Linux. Pseudocode tracing is covered in "Programming Basics (Pseudocode Tracing)", interrupts and register access with volatile in "Embedded Systems & Firmware", compiler optimizations in detail in "Compilers", and memory layout and linking in "Linkers, Loaders & Executables".

software-dev.name: Software Development and Project Management
software-dev.description: Learn software development and project management with multiple-choice questions: development processes such as the waterfall model, the V-model and agile development (Scrum), requirements and design (UML, module cohesion and coupling), test techniques (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, statement and branch coverage), Git and reviews, project management with WBS, critical paths, EVM and PERT, and SLAs and problem management.
software-dev.intro:
The quality and delivery of software depend less on how much code is written than on what is built in what order, how it is checked, and how its schedule and cost are managed. In development close to semiconductors and hardware, such as firmware, drivers, EDA scripts and verification environments, how well this is done also shapes the final product.
This topic covers ways of developing software such as the waterfall model and the V-model, Scrum, test-driven development and CI/CD; design ideas such as non-functional requirements, UML, and module cohesion and coupling; and test techniques such as equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis and branch coverage. It also covers the basics of project and service management, mainly through calculation questions: critical paths in arrow diagrams, three-point estimates, earned value management, risk responses, SLAs and problem management. It also helps with the software development and management sections of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations.
software-dev.blurb: Processes, testing, schedule and cost control

strategy.name: Business Strategy and Accounting Basics
strategy.description: Learn business strategy and accounting basics with multiple-choice questions: income statements and balance sheets, break-even analysis (variable cost ratio, contribution margin ratio, margin of safety), depreciation (straight-line and declining-balance), financial indicators such as ROE, inventory valuation, business strategy tools such as SWOT analysis, PPM, five forces analysis and the value chain, marketing concepts such as the 4Ps and the product life cycle, analysis methods such as ABC analysis, decision trees and linear programming, investment appraisal by NPV, and the basics of intellectual property and contracts.
strategy.intro:
The results of a semiconductor company depend not only on its technology but also on management decisions: which businesses to invest in and how much, at what price to sell, and how much must be made to earn a profit. The shape of the business, such as owning fabs that require huge capital investment or specializing in design as a fabless company, also affects the break-even point and resilience to economic cycles through the size of fixed costs and depreciation.
This topic covers accounting calculations such as reading the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement, break-even and target-profit sales, depreciation, ROE and the equity ratio, and inventory valuation; business strategy such as SWOT analysis, PPM, five forces analysis, the value chain, Porter's generic strategies and the experience curve; and marketing such as the 4Ps, STP, the product life cycle and pricing strategies. It also covers, mainly through calculation questions, ABC analysis, regression analysis, decision trees, the maximin principle, linear programming, investment appraisal by NPV, BPR and cloud services, copyright and patents, non-disclosure agreements and the idea of personal information. It also helps with the strategy sections of IT certification exams such as Japan's IT Passport, Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations.

service-management.name: IT Service Management and Systems Audit
service-management.description: Learn IT service management and systems audit with multiple-choice questions, including calculations: the approach of IT service management, SLAs and service level management, incident and problem management (workarounds and known errors), change and release management, configuration management (CMDB), the service desk and escalation, capacity management and availability calculations (MTBF and MTTR), business continuity plans (BCP), facilities such as UPS units and fire suppression, how a systems audit proceeds, audit trails and audit techniques, internal control and IT governance.
service-management.intro:
A system is not finished once it has been built and switched on. It has to run stably every day at the quality agreed with its users; when a failure occurs, service must be restored quickly, the cause removed so that the same failure does not recur, and changes made only after their impact has been checked. A systems audit then checks, from an independent standpoint, whether these management mechanisms really work.
This topic covers SLAs and service level management, availability calculations that take service hours and planned maintenance into account, the difference between incident management and problem management, change, release and configuration management (CMDB), the service desk and escalation, capacity management and MTBF/MTTR calculations, business continuity plans (BCP), and facilities such as UPS units and fire suppression. The second half deals with the independence of systems auditors, how an audit proceeds from the preliminary survey and main audit to the audit report and follow-up, audit evidence and audit trails, audit techniques such as the test data and ITF methods, Japan's System Management Standards and System Audit Standards, the objectives and basic components of internal control, segregation of duties, and IT governance. It helps with the management sections (service management and systems audit) of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations. Project management is covered in "Software Development and Project Management", and backups, RPO and RTO in "System Architecture and Reliability".
service-management.blurb: SLAs, incidents and problems, audits and internal control

system-architecture.name: System Architecture and Reliability
system-architecture.description: Learn system architecture and reliability with multiple-choice questions: system configurations such as client-server and three-tier systems, dual and duplex systems and hot standby, RAID capacity and tolerated failures, full, differential and incremental backups with RPO and RTO, fail-safe, fail-soft and fool-proof design, cloud and virtualization, SAN and NAS, PUE, and capacity planning.
system-architecture.intro:
How usable and how hard to stop an information system is depends not only on the performance of one computer but on how equipment is combined and how processing continues when something fails. This design matters especially for systems whose stopping directly affects production, such as a semiconductor fab's manufacturing execution system (MES) and the servers that collect equipment data.
This topic covers system configurations such as client-server, three-tier client-server, peer-to-peer, and batch and online processing, and redundancy concepts such as dual and duplex systems, hot standby, clusters and single points of failure. It also covers, with calculation questions, RAID capacity and the number of failures each level tolerates, backup restore procedures, RPO and RTO, reliability design such as fail-safe, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, live migration, SAN and NAS, PUE and UPS, and estimating the number of servers needed. It also helps with the system components sections of IT certification exams such as Japan's Fundamental and Applied Information Technology Engineer Examinations.

cloud-container.name: Cloud and Container Basics
cloud-container.description: Learn with multiple-choice questions about the namespaces and cgroups behind containers, images, layers and copy-on-write, Dockerfile instructions (RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY), the build cache and instruction order, publishing ports, volumes and bind mounts, tags and digests, multi-stage builds, Kubernetes Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress and Secrets, reconciliation and rolling updates, readiness and liveness probes, autoscaling calculations, requests and limits, the shared responsibility model, availability zones, serverless computing, storage types, the break-even point between pay-as-you-go and reservations, data transfer charges, IaC, immutable infrastructure, blue-green and canary releases, and observability.
cloud-container.intro:
