Many web services and corporate systems now run in the cloud as applications packaged in containers. A container isolates processes while sharing the host OS kernel; images are built with Docker, and platforms such as Kubernetes place containers on many machines, keep their number and update them.
This topic starts with namespaces and cgroups, image layers and copy-on-write, Dockerfile instructions and the build cache, publishing ports, volumes and bind mounts, tags and digests, and multi-stage builds, and then deals with Kubernetes Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress and Secrets, declaring a desired state and reconciliation, rolling update calculations, readiness and liveness probes, HorizontalPodAutoscaler calculations, and requests, limits and Pod placement. It goes on to check the shared responsibility model of the cloud, regions and availability zones, serverless computing and cold starts, block, file and object storage, pay-as-you-go charges and the break-even point of reservations, data transfer charges, IaC and immutable infrastructure, blue-green deployment and canary releases, building artifacts only once, configuration through environment variables, and observability. The values in the calculation questions, including those of the wrong choices, have been checked by computing them in Python. All prices are made-up values. The differences between hypervisors, containers and virtual machines are covered in "OS & Hardware"; IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, scale-out, redundancy, live migration and CDNs in "System Architecture and Reliability"; load balancers and sessions in "Web Technology Basics"; CI/CD in "Software Development and Project Management"; SLAs in "IT Service Management and Systems Audit"; and the shell and environment variables in "Linux and Command-Line Basics".

performance.name: Performance Analysis
performance.description: Learn performance analysis with multiple-choice questions: execution time = instruction count × CPI × cycle time, Amdahl's law calculations, benchmarking pitfalls, performance counters and identifying bottlenecks.
performance.intro:
A program's speed is the product of the number of instructions executed, the average cycles per instruction (CPI) and the cycle time. Improving one factor does not make the program faster if another gets worse. Amdahl's law adds that speeding up only part of a program leaves the rest to cap the overall speedup.
Comparing performance correctly requires care in choosing benchmarks, measuring them and averaging results. This topic covers ways to isolate bottlenecks, such as counting cache misses and branch mispredictions with CPU performance counters and using the roofline model to tell whether computation or memory is the limit.

hw-security.name: Hardware Security
hw-security.description: Learn hardware security with multiple-choice questions focused on principles and countermeasures: speculative-execution side channels (Spectre and Meltdown), power analysis and timing attacks, secure boot, TEEs, PUFs and hardware Trojans.
hw-security.intro:
Even when software is free of bugs, information can leak through properties of the hardware. Vulnerabilities known as Spectre and Meltdown exploit the fact that speculative execution and caches, which exist to improve performance, leave traces of data that should be invisible. Side-channel attacks can also infer cryptographic keys from tiny differences in power consumption or execution time.
Defensive technologies include secure boot, which starts only trusted software; trusted execution environments (TEEs), isolated even from the OS; PUFs, which use each chip's manufacturing variation like a fingerprint; and countermeasures against malicious circuits inserted during design or manufacturing (hardware Trojans). The goal is to understand principles and defenses, not attack procedures.
hw-security.blurb: Side channels, secure boot, TEE, PUF

hw-security-adv.name: Hardware Security: Advanced Topics and Trends
hw-security-adv.description: Learn with multiple-choice questions, including calculations: VM-based TEEs (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX and Arm CCA) and confidential computing, memory integrity protection and its cost, verifying attestation reports, GPU confidential computing, memory and control-flow protection with CHERI, MTE, pointer authentication and shadow stacks, Rowhammer with TRR, PRAC and the limits of ECC, MDS with retpoline and IBRS, the performance cost of mitigations, post-quantum cryptography in hardware (the number-theoretic transform, key sizes and implementation pitfalls), open roots of trust and DICE, secure firmware update, HBOMs, chiplet security, split manufacturing, IC camouflaging and logic locking, reverse engineering, FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria, PSA Certified and SESIP, authenticated debug and lifecycle states, scan chains, and fault injection by voltage glitches, lasers and electromagnetic pulses.
hw-security-adv.intro:
With the spread of cloud computing, AI and IoT devices, both what hardware security protects and how it is attacked have changed greatly. Confidential computing that protects data even from a cloud provider's administrators, hardware that stops pointer errors, cryptographic hardware for the era of quantum computers, and protecting a semiconductor supply chain involving many companies are major themes today. Building on the basics in "Hardware Security", this topic covers newer and deeper material.
It starts with confidential computing: the difference between VM-based and enclave-based TEEs and the trusted computing base (TCB), why integrity protection is needed in addition to encryption and a calculation of its storage cost, what a verifier checks in an attestation report, Arm CCA realms and confidential computing that includes GPUs. It continues with CHERI capabilities, a calculation of the probability that MTE tags match by chance, pointer authentication, and control-flow integrity through shadow stacks and protection of indirect branches. For attacks on DRAM it covers why Rowhammer becomes more likely with scaling, research that bypassed TRR, the limits of ECC, PRAC in DDR5 and a calculation relating refresh rate to activation counts; for transient execution attacks, MDS, retpoline and IBRS, and a calculation of the slowdown caused by mitigations. The second half covers speeding up polynomial multiplication with the number-theoretic transform, ML-KEM key sizes, implementation precautions for decapsulation, hardware designed so that cryptography can be replaced, OpenTitan and Caliptra, DICE, A/B updates with anti-rollback, HBOMs, trust between chiplets, split manufacturing, IC camouflaging and logic locking, and protecting keys against reverse engineering. It ends with FIPS 140-3 levels, Common Criteria EALs, composition in PSA Certified and SESIP, authenticated debug, lifecycle states and RMA, protecting scan chains, and fault injection by voltage glitches, lasers and electromagnetic pulses, including calculations of success probabilities and of the effect of countermeasures. The aim is to understand principles and countermeasures from the viewpoint of designers and defenders, not attack procedures. The values in the calculation questions, including those of the wrong choices, have been checked by computing them in Python. Product names, standard versions and years are given as of the time stated in each question. Side-channel attacks, Spectre, Meltdown and KPTI, power analysis, the basics of fault injection and Rowhammer, secure boot, TPMs, TEEs, TrustZone and enclaves, PUFs, true random number generators, hardware Trojans and disabling JTAG are covered in "Hardware Security"; the ML-KEM and ML-DSA standards and HSMs in "Applied Cryptography"; DRAM refresh and the name of the Rowhammer phenomenon in "DRAM"; chiplets and UCIe in "Advanced packaging (3D and chiplets)"; scan design in "Testing and inspection"; A/B firmware updates in "Embedded Systems & Firmware"; and ISO/SAE 21434 in "Automotive Semiconductors and Functional Safety".
hw-security-adv.blurb: Confidential computing, CHERI/MTE, Rowhammer, PQC hardware, supply chain

power-management.name: Power Management
power-management.description: Learn software-controlled power management with multiple-choice questions: dynamic and static power, DVFS and OS frequency control, power gating versus clock gating, sleep states and thermal throttling.
power-management.intro:
Both smartphone battery life and data-center electricity bills depend heavily on how chips use power. Power in CMOS circuits consists of dynamic power, consumed each time signals switch, and static power, consumed through leakage even when idle, and each calls for different countermeasures.
This topic covers how operating systems and firmware make use of hardware mechanisms such as DVFS, which lowers voltage and frequency to match the load; clock gating, which stops the clock to unused circuits; and power gating, which cuts off their supply entirely. It also covers CPU sleep and performance states and the idea behind thermal throttling when temperatures climb too high.
